rejected.title: Rhyme and rhythm
card: Rhyme
Rhyme is when words end with the same sound, such as "light" and "night". Rhyming words at the ends of lines link those lines together.
Rhythm
Rhythm is the beat of a poem. It comes from the pattern of stressed (strong) and unstressed (weak) syllables, such as da-DUM da-DUM.
A syllable is one beat of sound in a word. "Water" has two syllables: WA-ter. The first is stressed and the second is not.
Rhyme and rhythm together give a poem its sound. A steady beat with rhyming line endings can make a poem feel musical, like a song or a chant.

The number of lines in the poem

problems.detail: The card defines rhyme as words that 'end with the same sound', and the remember line says 'matching end sounds'. That is too loose. Rhyme needs the vowel sound and everything after it to match (light/night: -ight). By the card's wording, 'cat' and 'hot' would rhyme because both end in a t sound.

Under the card's definition ('end with the same sound'), smile, small, smell and simple all end with an l sound, so a student who follows the card closely could defend a distractor. The why says the endings of smile and small are different, but the card never explains that the vowel sound must match too.

The card calls a syllable 'one beat of sound in a word', but it also says rhythm is 'the beat' made by the pattern of stressed syllables. Using 'beat' for both every syllable and the stressed beat can confuse students about what is being counted, as in question b, where the claps fall on every second syllable.

proposal.title: Rhyme and rhythm
card: Rhyme
Words rhyme when the vowel sound and every sound after it match, as in light and night. Cat and hot do not rhyme: only the t sound matches.
Syllable
A syllable is a part of a word with one vowel sound. Water has two syllables, WA-ter: the first is stressed (said strongly) and the second is unstressed (said lightly).
Rhythm
Rhythm is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line, such as da-DUM da-DUM. The stressed syllables are the beat you could tap or clap.
Rhyming words at line endings link those lines. Together with a steady rhythm, rhyme can make a poem sound musical, like a song or a chant.
proposal.remember: Rhyme matches the vowel sound and what follows it. Rhythm is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables.

a.q: Which pair of words rhymes, so it could link two line endings?
a.why: Smile and while share the same vowel sound and the l sound after it, so they rhyme. Smile and small both end with an l sound, but their vowel sounds are different, so they do not rhyme.
a.clue: Check the vowel sound, not just the last sound.

b.q: Mia claps as she reads this line aloud: "The WIND blew COLD a-CROSS the HILL". Her claps land on the parts in capitals, every second syllable. What is she finding?
opts: The syllable count of the line
The rhyming words in the line
b.why: Mia claps only on the stressed syllables, so she is following the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables, which is the rhythm. She is not counting syllables, because she skips every unstressed one, and rhyme is about matching sounds at line endings, not inside one line.
b.clue: Does she clap on every syllable, or only the strong ones?
